abstract: This paper investigates the widely held assumption that exposure to opposing political views on social media reduces polarization by counteracting 'echo chambers.' Through a field experiment, the authors paid Democrats and Republicans to follow Twitter bots that retweeted messages from elected officials and opinion leaders holding opposing political views. Contrary to expectations, exposure to opposing views did not reduce polarization and in some cases increased it, particularly among Republicans.
key_claims: The common assumption that exposing people to opposing views on social media will reduce political polarization is not supported by experimental evidence.
Exposure to opposing partisan views can, in some cases, increase rather than decrease political polarization.
The polarizing effect of cross-partisan exposure differs by party affiliation, with Republicans showing a stronger reaction.
methods: A field experiment involving a large sample of self-identified Democrats and Republicans who use Twitter.
Participants were offered financial compensation to follow a bot that retweeted messages from elected officials and opinion leaders with opposing political views.
Measurement of participants' political attitudes to assess changes in conservatism/liberalism following the intervention.
findings: Republican participants who followed a liberal bot expressed substantially more conservative views after the intervention.
Democratic participants exhibited a slight (though less pronounced) increase in liberal attitudes after following a conservative bot.
Overall, exposure to opposing views failed to reduce polarization and tended to reinforce or intensify existing partisan positions.
contributions: Provides causal, experimental evidence challenging the 'echo chamber' remedy narrative that increased cross-partisan exposure reduces polarization.
Highlights asymmetric partisan responses to counter-attitudinal information on social media.
Informs debates on the design of social media platforms and interventions aimed at reducing political polarization.
framing: The paper positions itself within research on political polarization, social media echo chambers, and the psychology of attitude change, directly testing a popular policy assumption that greater exposure to opposing views depolarizes citizens. It draws on theories of motivated reasoning and identity-protective cognition to interpret why counter-attitudinal exposure may backfire.
